hook_text: In 1948, the world promised that every person is born equal, and in the same year South Africa chose the opposite road.
clip_script: The world had just survived its darkest war. Tens of millions dead. Six million Jews murdered in the Holocaust, step by step, using laws. So the nations of the world made a promise. On 10 December 1948, in Paris, they adopted the Universal Declaration of Human Rights. Thirty articles. Article 1: all human beings are born free and equal in dignity and rights. No slavery. No torture. A fair trial. Freedom to speak, to move, to marry, to vote, to learn. Forty-eight countries voted yes. Eight held back. One of them was South Africa. Because that same year, the National Party had won power and begun to build apartheid. It would take almost fifty years before those thirty promises were written into South Africa's own Constitution.
visual_style: Black-and-white footage of post-war ruins; the UN General Assembly in Paris, 1948; Eleanor Roosevelt holding a poster of the Declaration; the words of Article 1 appearing on screen; a 1948 South African election poster; the 1996 Constitution being signed.
pacing: Measured, with a sharp turn at South Africa's abstention.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson to learn what the Universal Declaration says and why it mattered for South Africa.
